paragraphs.heading: Seeing it with my own eyes
paragraphs.edited: One of my dreams has been to go back to the Holy Land. I had a chance to visit Israel with my family when I was about 10 years old, and I'll never forget being at the Temple Mount, walking through Hezekiah's tunnel, and of course having a chance to ride on a camel. But going back recently with a student group that I led was life-changing. On the recent trip I had a chance to take a boat ride on the Sea of Galilee, visit Beth Shean, where the Bible describes that the body of King Saul was hung, see the remains of Jericho with my own eyes, and I got to go to the pool of Bethesda, where John 5 describes that Jesus healed a paralytic. Seeing many of these places with my own eyes really made the biblical stories come alive.

paragraphs.heading: Does archaeology prove the Bible?
paragraphs.edited: But it got me thinking, more than ever, how does the biblical account match up with the archaeological record? Maybe you've heard people say that archaeology proves the Bible is true. Well, that is certainly an overstatement. After all, many fictional stories can be based upon real people, events, and places. But what archaeology can do is show that the biblical writers were careful. You see, the archaeological record can be part of a larger case showing that the Bible is trustworthy.

paragraphs.heading: Two things to keep in mind
paragraphs.edited: Before we take a look at two of my favorite examples of archaeological evidence that support the reliability of the Bible, keep a couple of things in mind. First off, the archaeological record is incomplete. There are many things we haven't found. In fact, there are many things we probably will never find. There are a lot of things that have just disintegrated and been destroyed. So if you expect the archaeological record to be complete, you're going to be disappointed. But second, taken as a whole, the archaeological record supports the stories as found in the Bible. There are many, many findings that support that the biblical writers got it correct. paragraphs.heading: The pool with five colonnades
paragraphs.edited: First, in John chapter 5, John reports one of the most famous miracles of Jesus, where he heals a paralytic in Bethesda at a pool that's surrounded by five colonnades. Now, critics almost unanimously dismiss this as being a fabrication, because it's such an unusual description. Yet when archaeologists dug in Bethesda, guess what they found? They found exactly what John described, a pool surrounded by five colonnades. And I got to visit Bethesda and see this with my own eyes.

paragraphs.heading: More examples
paragraphs.edited: Examples like this could be multiplied. For example, recently a pottery inscription has been found with the name Goliath that dates to the time of the biblical account. And in northern Israel another inscription has been found that refers to the house of David. And an ossuary has been discovered that seems to be of the historical figure Caiaphas, who was the high priest when Jesus was condemned to death. The archaeological record has consistently provided support for the reliability of the Bible. When you combine the archaeological findings with the willingness of the apostles to die for their belief, the manuscript evidence, and fulfilled prophecy, we have a strong case for the trustworthiness of the Scriptures.

paragraphs.heading: A conversation in Israel
paragraphs.edited: On my recent trip to Israel, I had a chance to meet with a friend of mine who at the time was a PhD student in archaeology at Hebrew University, and he took me and the students up to see the cave where they first discovered the Dead Sea Scrolls. And I asked him, I said, in Israel as a whole, what do people think about the historical Jesus? What he said surprised me. He said there is general agreement on the basic facts around the story of Jesus, and certainly that he existed. He said there's general agreement about where Jesus was born, about where he grew up, where he ministered, and where he died.

paragraphs.heading: Spiritual blindness
paragraphs.edited: And so I asked him, I said, so why do you think more people don't believe? And I'll never forget what he said. He said, I really believe it's spiritual blindness. You see, God is not going to force anybody to believe, but to those with eyes to see and with ears to hear, God has made himself known. The question is, are you going to believe the gospel, apply it to your life, and live it out? What could be more important than that?
